desc:
People wait at a river bank; weights[i] is the weight of person i. You have boats boats, each used for a single trip. A boat carries at most two people, and the total weight on one boat must not exceed limit.

Not everyone may fit. Return the largest number of people that can be carried across.

weights = [5, 1, 4, 2, 3], limit = 6, boats = 2
boats: (1,4) and (2,3)  ->  4 people
result = 4

weights = [7, 8, 2], limit = 7, boats = 3
the person of weight 8 can never ride
result = 2
hints: If you decide to carry exactly m people, which m people should they be?
Replacing a carried person with a lighter one who stays behind never hurts, so the carried group can always be the m lightest people. Also, if m people fit in the boats, then m - 1 fit too.

Sort and binary search m. For a given m, the lightest m people need at most boats boats if the heaviest of them weighs at most limit and the classic two-pointer pairing (lightest with heaviest if they fit, otherwise heaviest alone) uses at most boats boats.
editorial: Sort the weights. If some set of people can cross, swapping any member for a lighter person outside the set keeps all boat loads within the limit, so the lightest m people are always the best choice for a group of size m. A smaller group of the lightest people is also never harder than a larger one, so feasibility is monotone in m.

Feasibility of m: the heaviest of the group must satisfy w[m-1] ≤ limit, and the minimum number of boats for the group, computed by the standard greedy (heaviest person takes the lightest remaining one if they fit, otherwise travels alone), must be at most boats. Binary search the largest feasible m.
Each check is a linear two-pointer pass, so the total time is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n log n) for the binary search.
